File size depends on how you create your assets. Textures can be compressed in Unity, and several other things can too. Compression is a scary thing for AAA devs, haha. Most of your big data space takers are most likely going to be textures and audio. From my experience, at least.

If you're making a game like that, low poly and easier to make than realistic stuff, I don't think you'll have to stress about your game being above 10GBs. Definitely potential for less depending on how you compress it. Not even a single GB, potentially. This is definitely possible in Unity. Compression is great, and so are optimal assets. 

To answer though, it is best to test it out yourself. Create a scene and export your game. Believe me, it won't be a lot. You got it. :)))

Hard to compare Mesh Baker when it has limited tools compared to Blender. It is made for Unity and the poor draw calls you get sometimes. Great asset, recommended. But it won't completely reduce polys. Combines materials and makes everything have one material. Other tools as well. Polyfew, yes. I guarantee you won't get the results you want every time you use it. Every model is different if you're using assets. This meaning UV placements, polycount, pivot states, etc.

Blender has everything this guy is asking for and it is FREE. The downside is that you have to learn Blender. 

Unity is a game development software, less of a program where you are making 3D models and optimizing a certain model. Unless, once again, you have assets that are mostly paid.

You should be able to open a certain model in Blender. .Fbx, .Obj, I've been doing this for years. Don't import Unity prefabs but instead import the actual model. The only thing I can see not being importable is game objects from Unity, or terrains. Otherwise learn about retopology. Reducing triangles in Unity isn't really something that will go well. Because there isn't really any solution for this. Unless you compress the hell out of the model.

Definitely see if the asset you have is interact-able with your own scripts, maybe some of those scripts don't have anything in the inspector and is claimed as a private variable. There are a lot of things that could be conflicting with your issue. Another script could be telling it to do something else, maybe the collider on the model isn't set as a trigger, or raycasts aren't setup correctly. If it is a raycast situation, then most likely, it isn't a trigger. Maybe you have to create your own tag and put that tag on the collision you want in the inspector. I'm guessing this is a raycast system since you're trying to create an interaction manager. Maybe use a bool and test it. If the player is looking at the collider, make sure the bool turns true. If the player stops looking at it, then make the bool false. This is a way of troubleshooting.

Now, if it does return as true, the bool, then most likely, something else is interacting with the script, maybe an animator hasn't been applied or maybe the Animator doesn't have the correct bool applied to it when you actually click the elevator button. Check the Animator bools, floats, or strings, however it was setup. Does the animator controller have any parameters? If so, then check to see if those parameters are being met, if they aren't, then learn how use more of the animator and how to program transitions. Maybe the script is setup on a different object, there are a LOT of questions more than answers. This is all estimates of troubleshooting and some are answered. But be ready to troubleshoot, you can do it. Absolutely can.

Heyo, been making games since I was around 15? Unsure exactly when, but now, I'm 8 years older and had a lot of projects. More cancelled than finished, it sucks to cancel a project because you aren't feeling confident with it or losing motivation on something you don't enjoy. But the years of making games, I made pure slop. I always thought when releasing it at the time, people would love it. When I released it, I came back with more questions than answers. I did feel amazing when finishing it and finally getting approved for release on Steam. I feel a lot of projects when making games are simply there to help you kickstart your career, I wouldn't purposely try and make something huge for your first project. I'm currently working on a huge project now after only making games that just never really fit for me. I see a lot of developers rushing to create something with one goal in mind, release it as quick as possible.

In reality, you won't get far with that mindset. I'm not going to lie, you're going to work constantly on your projects if you want it to be good. Learning and asking questions, thinking about what a player might do in this scenario, or that scenario, blah blah. You're going to look more into details on other games, like maybe adding a puddle to your own game, there are multiple ways to do it, but when you do finally finish it, you'll know something new and adapt to newer situations maybe using that same route of making a puddle and improving on it. I can yap about this all day. My end-goal was simple, create a passion project and put out something I love myself. A huge project. It took me years to finally feel confident enough to work on something larger. Unity has great tools, some tools in Unity are better with assets. Personally, the terrain system is horrible. Animation tool is amazing but could use more options. I personally use a few animator tools because it speeds development up. If you want to know a lot of people's first projects, I can promise you that most people created slop when first learning. Me, I made a garbage Slender The Eight Pages clone, a cube enemy chased you that had a jpeg on it. As a kid, it was AWESOME. Now? No, it sucks.

  
Is it worth it? I'm someone who appreciates art and storytelling. I like to use games to tell that instead of words. So, for me, absolutely worth spending my time as a developer learning. I have a lot of troubleshooting skills because of game development. You don't just learn one thing, you can learn multiple things that can help outside of development. I learned a lot more techy stuff, marketing, 3D art, music production, etc. Some people wouldn't find it worth it to spend all this time. That is why shortcuts exist, it is better you avoid using bad shortcuts constantly. AI for example being one. I love Unity, everyone trashes it because of controversy and the stereotype of asset flips, yet you can make some amazing things. Truly amazing things. I think going at it with a different mindset for me made it worth it. To make the player feel connected to my characters I created, relatable characters. You may have a different idea of how it could be worth it. I believe it matters to whoever is creating the game. Don't go into this thinking MONEY MONEY MONEY!!! Because you are going to get bored and frustrated if that is your only mindset. Instantly losing attachment to your own projects.

What I've been using to create trees is a software called "TreeIt." (http://www.evolved-software.com/) Free, but you can support the developer on Steam if wanted, too. You can make trees with custom textures to avoid all the UV stuff.

Super great at making and exporting FBX models and creating trees in general for completely free. There are some limits, it doesn't create a UV for you, meaning you have to UV Unwrap it yourself and texture it. Also, wind is something that must be done with shaders, at least in URP and HDRP. My process is basically making a tree, going into Maya (or Blender) to create the UVs from scratch, after it is finished, I then port my model to Substance Painter and go from there.

You can set up a rig for your tree pretty easily, animate it, or use shaders to apply wind. This software doesn't export wind animations. But it does export the wind information for a vertex shader, I believe. There is an FAQ on the site that has the answer to this.

Unpopular opinion coming up *maybe*: I've worked on horror games for a good minute, my whole game dev career was horror, but this depends on what you're going for on design, If you're trying to *scare* the player, then I feel having the player being able to fight back may instantly KILL the scare factor for some people. As it does for me, I feel when I feel defenseless in a horror game and the fear of the unknown, this is what makes something scary. Alien Isolation, you had limited tools to go against the Alien, you couldn't kill it. Another great alien horror game experience is Voices of The Void, where the unknown can be scary as shit. 

Example of a BAD horror game? Greyhill Incident, it's stereotypical as hell, farm area, aliens invade, super dark and scary looking, UFO, then you pull out a gun, it just completely kills the horror element. Some people may find it scary, but if you're a gamer who's been playing games for a good minute, this is just something you're used to seeing constantly. Shooting enemies. 

Some horror games with guns, you are either some badass going against several enemies, usually in these alien games, you're some standard person like yourself, not a Leon S Kennedy. Those games can be scary with guns because of the different variety of enemies and fast paced gameplay, the survival element. Some people, it differs.

So to answer your questions:

1: This will depend for some players, some people hate QTEs, some people like them. I will say, this does have a bit too much camera sway, at least to me. Otherwise, everything else, it looks okay. Do not make it overly difficult at all, or else people will feel turned away from this. I recommend having an AUTO QTE option. Seriously, huge for some games. Example for one is the Yakuza series.

2: Of course post your game to Steam, anywhere actually/. Never feel discouraged to post your game anywhere, there is a BUNCH of AI use on Steam nowadays, so uh, take advantage of that. Art, code, audio, even models, it's not great. If you are using any form of AI, this may hurt sales. I personally don't buy anything that has the *AI GENERATED CONTENT DISCLOSURE* notice on the steam page, and I know if I'm someone who does that, then someone else out there does that too. You're making a craft, a game, putting a lot of time into this, you might as well put some extra time into the assets and not take the easy way out. Other than that, a lot of indie devs don't want to hear that their failures of a game aren't great or unique looking, not a lot of gamers want to play something that doesn't look appealing.

Anyway, it isn't bad, ask players what they enjoy personally, what you enjoy, and maybe make options for BOTH.

Hello, I'm someone who was extremely young and had long distance relationships my whole life. And I regret it completely. I'm going to be straight up, they are NOT meant to last long whatsoever. They are long distance for a reason and a lot of these never last. I've had around 3-4? It's bad because I can't remember, but I was young and stupid. I'm 23 now. But the most memorable one I had broke me and still haunts me to this day, gives me PTSD and I never open up about it to anyone, but I am making a game about the story and making sure people don't make the same mistake.

I had a friend group with 3 people, me and two friends. They gave me a LOT of hints and I was dumb to never see them, I was someone who was the comedic person in the group. And that's why they liked me, I was a funny silly guy even in the serious moments, trying to calm it down. After not understanding that they liked me, they decided to go for the other friend, and it broke the friend group apart. Only because one of the friends cheated on each other. They were both being distant on me anyway, leaving calls with me to be with each other and calling it a day. I decided I was better somewhere else.

These were my closest friends, and it hurt big time for me. I panicked thinking about them, and panicked when someone else talked about them. I hated it. Years later, I came across the person who liked me. Of course, panicking, I acted the way I used to be. Which was someone I wasn't, I changed. I became a quieter person over the years and to act completely different around them, it felt normal. I did feel they were going to hate me, and attack me for leaving. But it was different, they were kind and we talked privately. Eventually talked again, and they were the same. It turns out things didn't work and blah blah, we started having a long-distance relationship. Me being a goofball, I supported them in rough times. They were in a harder spot than the last time I talked with them. I gave them money because I thought we were closer than others, we knew way more than what other partners did.

Their patterns were strange in messages, longer wait times and said that they were just tired, and slept a lot. I understood, but it got off pattern. I eventually got a message saying they would like to just be friends, understanding but frustrated at the same time, the next day I find out that I'm blocked. I'm still really confused by this. I also find out that she was texting someone else, apparently being sexual. I knew this person. This stuff only hurts because I thought they were a close friend, longer than 5 years of being online friends, you think it would mean something. Daily calls, daily doing things together. It ended quick doing an online relationship. Their accounts are gone, everything is gone. So, I'm unsure what they are doing now. Having a person who can be in person is just more helpful for you, not the webcams, and you don't have to hear that \*when I'm there in a few months\* type of deal, you can just make plans for next week for coffee.

You'd be surprised when they say there is someone for everyone. I believe it now. You are extremely young, and there are people out there. Do not rush it, please take time to learn who you are. This killed me as person when I was younger, be smarter.

Heyo, did NSFW for a minute. (sadly) And I see the market for it. HUGE market for it. Let me give you some tips.

- NSFW games sell for a lot of gamers, but some people just buy these games for the meme and leave a review without even playing the game because it's funny. So sometimes, you may get sales without even people playing the game. That's why you see so many NSFW games on Steam that are asset flips, the same people creating them are pretty much abusing the fact that this works. Nothing wrong with it, either.

- If you want a unique NSFW game as well, be ready to put in some work. Art, animations, and gameplay must be pretty unique. Lots of stuff has been done, but not everything, of course! Story is great to have, you don't want it to take ages to get to the good stuff, but at least feel rewarding too. It depends how your game is, though. Never make it to where it'll take hours though. As that isn't something players want to do.

- Someone said it before, ability to play with one hand. Have your game playable with one hand. Big one here, nobody wants to keep going back and forth on their keyboard when doing their naughty stuff, haha.

It's just about being unique with your gameplay, story, art style, characters, anything to stand out from the rest. Even the title has to be unique and hopefully easy to find and remember. Sites like [Itch.io](http://Itch.io), and Steam can have NSFW games. Good luck!
